ops.text:
RESOLVED to (b), a test fix — the (b)/(c) fork does not need an owner call.

Reading the contract settles it. control.go:67-69:

  // ReapTerminated is reached only by owned-child settlement ladders that
  // delivered signals; Drain and Settle never signal and never return it.

ReapTerminated promises signal DELIVERY, not that the process left the table. Only ReapAbsent
("the pinned identity was observed gone") promises absence, and the failing assertion at
acceptance_test.go:163 accepts EITHER before asserting !alive(orphan).

And the helper conflates two states: own_test.go:329 is

  func alive(pid int) bool { return syscall.Kill(pid, 0) == nil }

kill(pid, 0) succeeds against a ZOMBIE — a process that has exited but whose parent has not
reaped it. The orphan in this test belongs to a prior generation and is reparented, so a zombie
window is its normal path out, not an anomaly. alive() reports a dead process as alive for the
whole of it.

So the test asserts a property stronger than the contract it just checked, using a predicate that
cannot distinguish dead-and-unreaped from running. The production code is not wrong, which removes
the reason (c) was ever on the table: nothing here suggests Owned.Close or the reclaim ladder
should promise more than they do.

Under load the zombie window widens, which is exactly the load correlation already measured
(0/60 idle; the Lane D3 refuter hit it in 2 of 3 full-suite runs while another gate battery
competed for CPU).

Fix: poll to a bound instead of sampling once, which covers both the zombie window and the
signal-delivery window. If a stronger assertion is wanted, alive() must read process state through
the kern.proc sysctls internal/proc already binds, rather than kill(pid, 0).
